unresolvedReferences.description: Gu Kai (曾孫楷) is listed as Gu Hun's great-grandson; the two intervening generations are named only in the biography in later chunks, so no intermediary rows are created here.
Kou Jun and Yao Xiong are listed as grandsons (孫) of Kou Zan and Yao Xuan; the intervening parents are not named in this chunk.
Gu Kai is Gu Hun's great-grandson (曾孫), but the text does not say through which son and grandson; no intermediaries are created.
The son for whom Gongsun Biao sought Feng Kai's niece is not named; 從女 may be a brother's or cousin's daughter, so no intermediary parent is created.
The emperor (帝) who wished to pardon the Feng clan is identified with Mingyuan only by narrative context.
The Dingling chieftain who cursed Gongsun Gui and his murdered mother are unnamed; no person rows are created.
The chief clerk (主簿) whose report is cited in Xiaowen's mourning edict is unnamed.
Taiwu's Liangzhou campaign is not dated in the text; Zhi's episode is bounded only by Taiwu's reign (423-452).
The Prince of Qi Commandery (齊郡王) whom Li Yu served as Companion is not named; no person row is created.
Li Yihui is Li Jiao's grandson; the intervening generation is not named.
Li Jingru is Yihui's grandson (其孫); the intervening generation is not named. Yuan Dan's succession to Yuan Yi is stated only as 嗣位.
Li Yu's children (妻子) are unnamed.
The Chaibi campaign is not dated in the text; bounded by Daowu's reign.
Li Zhaohui's wife and children are unnamed.
The battle at Canhe is not dated in the text; bounded by Murong Chui's reign (384-396).
道武即位 is taken as Daowu's imperial accession (398), following the Canhe capture; the text does not give the year.
The eldest sons of Jia Xiu and Gao Yun are unnamed.
The five emperors Jia Xiu served are not named.
The pacification of the Three Qin and the Gai Wu campaign are not dated in the text; bounded by Taiwu's reign.
Dou Jin's other sons who perished are not named.
Whether Dou Zun or Sengyan was dismissed (坐免) is grammatically ambiguous; attributed to Zun with strongly-inferred certainty.
Li Xin's elder brothers (諸兄) are unnamed.
Li Fu's brothers (敷兄弟) are referred to collectively and not named here.
Li Xin's daughter married to Pei You is not named; no row is created.
The son who buried Han Yanzhi (子從其言) is not named; he may or may not be Han Qiao, so no link is made.
Han Yanzhi's grandsons (其孫數家) are unnamed.
The zh text reads 乙太安二年; 乙 is taken as a conversion error for 以, giving Tai'an 2 (456).
Liu Yu's campaign against Sima Xiuzhi is not dated in the text; bounded by Emperor An of Jin's reign.
Mao Xiuzhi's three other sons who stayed in the south are unnamed.
The zh reads 涼武昭王霸; King Wuzhao of Western Liang is usually named Li Gao (暠). The name 霸 is recorded as written.
Li Bao is Tang He's sister's son (甥); the sister and Li Bao's father are not named.
An Ji's capture of Huatai and Yan Ling's surrender are not dated in the text.
經二十年 counts from the fall of Western Liang (421); the Tangs' later campaigns are bounded by Taiwu's reign only.
The zh gives 周公萬度歸; the title is recorded as written (other sources give 成周公).
The son of Wei Shu's host whose death is alluded to is unnamed.
The sixteen posthumously honoured Kou clansmen are unnamed.
The en 'He sent a memorial' has no name in the zh (遣使表狀); not linked as a name.
Zuxun's father is Kou Zhen (named in the previous chunk); here he is referred to only via 子 and 父母.
The Dacheng rebellion is not dated in the text; bounded by Xuanwu's and Xiaoming's reigns.
The capture of Cao Yanzhi falls during Kou Jun's Liangzhou governorship (from 529) but its year is not given.
恭帝三年 is taken as year 3 of Emperor Gong of Western Wei (556); that emperor used no era name.

The text says Fan served the Eastern Palace in Taiwu's time and was ennobled when 'Taiwu took the throne'; the sequence is chronologically awkward (possibly an error for a later accession), so the accession date is marked uncertain.
Who sent the seventy garrison soldiers is not stated; the context implies Kou Zuli.
敗退 at Guoyang is ambiguous (the Wei army or the enemy); Daoyuan's pursuit implies the enemy withdrew.
The two sons killed with Daoyuan are unnamed; recorded as a family summary rather than as persons.
The source text of this unit is corrupt and unreadable; nothing extracted.
范弟道峻 reads as 'Fan's younger brother Daojun', but the 道- generation name suggests Daojun was Daoyuan's brother (Fan's son); the sibling link to Fan is marked uncertain.
The fall of Pingyang is dated only by Erzhu Rong's march on the capital (528).
The emperor who issued the edict returning Han Wu's gifts is not named.
Xiong's father Rong is named only in the preceding read-only unit; recorded with a mention exception.
Yao Xiong's Eastern Wei campaigns (s0822-s0847) are not individually dated; bounded by Xiaowu's flight (534) and Xiong's death (542).
友 before 外兵參軍 is unclear (possibly 'friend' or a textual corruption); Wang Hengjia is treated as the Outer Troops Adjutant.
禽丞伯 ('captured Cheng Bo') is ambiguous; no person created.
秀 is taken as Jia Xiu because the commentary follows biography order (after Jia Yi); Han Xiu is named separately in s0894.
崔公 (Lord Cui) is not further identified in this chunk; taken as Yuan Shi's patron, probably Cui Hao.
脩之 is taken as Mao Xiuzhi, the biography subject, rather than Zhu Xiuzhi.
構崇 appears to be a corruption of 柳崇 (Liu Chong); only 崇 is linked.
